newsitem.title: CHILE: FEATURE-Chilean women face threats, jail for abortion.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Chilean women face threats, jail for abortion.

text.p: Some women are shouted at and insulted by doctors, others are handcuffed to their hospital beds, some have guards posted in their rooms and hundreds are arrested every year.

Their crime was to have an abortion, which in Roman Catholic Chile is a punishable offence. This deeply conservative country is among the few in the world to outlaw abortion in absolutely all cases. Most countries allow it in special circumstances including rape, serious malformation of the foetus or if the mother's life is in danger.

Irma, whose case was recounted in a new study called "Women on Trial for Abortion," is typical of the abuse that women who have had botched abortions can receive in Chilean hospitals. She came in bleeding from a backroom abortion after two months of pregnancy, with swollen legs and intense pain in her left arm, the report said.

A nurse berated her and even the man who swept her room taunted and insulted her. A prison guard checked up on her every day and all her visitors had their bags searched. When she came around in intensive care, a court clerk told her she was under arrest. As soon as doctors gave the all-clear, guards hustled her off to jail to await trial, wearing only a nightshirt and underwear.
"I felt my whole world was falling apart. I would have preferred to have died at that moment," the study quoted the mother of two children as saying.
Not surprisingly, most women who have been through a bungled abortion stay away from hospitals or do not go until their symptoms have grown much worse.
"Women are often petrified to go to a hospital as they know they will be treated badly," Lt. Col. Eugenia Gonzalez of the Carabineros police force said.

Despite the ban, several studies have shown that Chile has one of Latin America's highest abortion rates with at least 150,000 women a year undergoing abortions in clandestine clinics. France, with about five times Chile's population, has 170,000 abortions a year, according to figures just published in Que Pasa news magazine. The figures also showed Chile with a higher per capita abortion rate than the United States.

Changing the abortion laws remains a political taboo in Chile, where the ban's supporters vociferously defend a foetus' right to life and question the accuracy of abortion statistics. "I do not share the idea that a mother has rights over her foetus," righwing Sen. Olga Feliu said. "Abortion is a crime and must be prohibited."

The main cause of the problem is that teenagers are having sex before they can fully assume the consequences of it, Feliu told Reuters. "We must discourage youngsters from having precocious sex lives, which leads to abortions, sexually transmitted diseases and AIDS."

Chile's conservative social mores are not limited to abortion. Divorce is illegal, sodomy a crime and film censorship is common on cable TV. The movie "The Last Temptation of Christ" is banned in Chile by a court order because it is considered blasphemous.

Police carry out undercover work to identify illegal abortion clinics but the task is slow as most women are unwilling to cooperate, Gonzalez said. Those who do are usually released from detention within five days in exchange for reporting on the abortion doctor.
Most women receive suspended sentences but many spend at least a month behind bars before their case is tried, Lidia Casas, author of the study that reported Irma's case, said.

In Chile, abortion was allowed until 1989 in cases when a mother's life was in danger as a result of her pregnancy. But the then-military government tightened the law, arguing that medical science had advanced so far that a woman's life would never be in danger from a pregnancy.

A report from the New York-based Alan Guttmacher Institute called "Clandestine Abortion: a Latin American Reality" showed that 35 percent of all Chilean pregnancies were aborted in 1990, the highest rate in the region. It said 31 percent of Brazilian pregnancies ended in abortion, followed by Peru with 30 percent and the Dominican Republic with 28 percent.

The Catholic Church's influence, political unwillingness to debate the issue and the lack of a strong feminist movement means there is little chance of easing the ban on abortion anytime soon, experts said.
